conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team doctors. You've been admitted for severe abdominal pain. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, the pain in my upper belly’s been getting worse over the past few days. It’s sharp, comes and goes, but lately it hasn’t let up. I’ve also been nauseous and threw up a couple times.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Given your history of chronic pancreatitis, this sounds like another flare-up. We’ll run some tests, but it looks like acute on chronic pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it because of those stones again? Last time they said the duct was blocked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your recent MRCP showed two stones in the pancreatic duct—one in the neck and one in the mid-body. They’re causing a blockage, and the duct has widened from 4mm to 10mm. That’s likely why the pain is so severe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s the plan? More ERCP? Last time the stent made things worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not doing another ERCP this time. Because of your history and the size of the stones, the team is planning a Puestow procedure—a surgery to drain the pancreas. It’s scheduled for next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Surgery? I thought we could just remove the stones like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We could try, but you’ve had multiple ERCPs already, and the stones keep coming back. The Puestow will create a permanent drainage path, which should help prevent future flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about pain now? It’s really bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now, you’re getting IV fluids and Dilaudid through a PCA pump—press the button when you need it. We switched from regular IV doses because the PCA gives better control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I pressed it a few times. It’s helping, but not completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Give it a little time. We’ll keep monitoring. We also started you on omeprazole to protect your stomach and pancreatic enzymes with meals to help digestion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on those already at home. Should I keep taking duloxetine and lisinopril?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve continued all your home meds except painkillers—we’re managing that here. Your blood pressure and mood meds are important to keep stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable. The lipase was low on admission, but that’s common in chronic cases. Your glucose is 188, so we’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that high? I have diabetes, but I thought I had it under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a bit elevated, but not dangerous. Stress and illness can raise blood sugar. We’re not starting insulin—you’re tolerating sips, and we’ll advance your diet slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat real food soon? I’m tired of just sipping water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to move you to clear liquids today. If you tolerate that, tomorrow you can start a low-fat diet. Pancreatitis means we have to go slow with food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Low-fat, right. I remember from last time. No fried stuff, no heavy meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And keep taking your pancreatic enzymes with every meal—they help your body digest food properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well—no vomiting, pain is better with oral meds now. We’re switching you from the PCA to oral Dilaudid as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I don’t like the IV thing anyway. Can I walk around more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please do. Ambulating helps prevent blood clots, especially since you have a history of DVT. We’ve been giving you heparin shots and you’ve been using the compression boots—great job.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last hospital stay. I’ll keep walking the hall a few times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We also did a chest X-ray today as part of your pre-op workup. It came back normal, which is good before surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is everything looking okay for the surgery next week?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. ECG was normal, labs are stable, and you’re moving your bowels and urinating normally. All signs point to you being ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re being discharged today. You’ve been on a low-fat diet, pain is controlled with oral meds, and you’re walking well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do before surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Resume all your regular medications except NSAIDs—no ibuprofen, naproxen, or aspirin. They can increase bleeding risk. Take omeprazole, simvastatin, and your other meds as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the Dilaudid? I still have some pain at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re getting a 30-day supply with no refills. Use it only as needed. Also, we’re adding Colace for constipation, which can happen with pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take it easy, rest, and keep walking. No driving, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Don’t drive or operate heavy machinery while on pain meds. And avoid lifting anything heavy until your surgeon clears you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll follow up with my PCP and the surgeon. Is there anything else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just stay hydrated, keep eating low-fat, and call if you develop fever, severe pain, or vomiting. Otherwise, see you next week for surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Doctor. I appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You’ve done really well. Take care, and we’ll see you soon for the Puestow.
